ARE.story:
The record for the United Arab Emirates covers abuse of children by Emirati personnel in the war in Yemen, the country's place as the base of a messaging platform used to share abuse images, and a very high number of online abuse reports for which there is no survey data.

In Yemen, the Group of Eminent Experts, a panel set up by the UN Human Rights Council, reported in September 2019 that UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa had raped a boy. The same report found that the Security Belt Forces and Yemen's 35th Armoured Brigade had raped boys, and the Group said its figures were a small sample.

Telegram, a messaging platform, has its operational centre in Dubai. In August 2024 a Paris investigating judge placed its founder, Pavel Durov, under formal investigation on charges that included suspected complicity in running a platform that allowed images of child sexual abuse, and refusing to give information to the authorities. A BBC investigation that month found Telegram had ignored repeated requests to join NCMEC, the US centre that receives reports of online child abuse, or the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF), a British charity that finds and removes abuse images. In December 2024 Telegram agreed to use the IWF's lists of known images to detect them in public parts of the platform; the IWF said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse imagery on Telegram since 2022.

The UAE also takes part in police work against online abuse. It was one of ten members of the Virtual Global Taskforce, an alliance of police forces, whose 2015 Operation Atlas arrested 303 people and identified 106 child victims.

Technology companies sent NCMEC 137,578 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse linked to the UAE in 2024, or 1,252.3 per 100,000 people. These are reports of suspected material, and Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey of the Middle East and North Africa that could show how many children are abused. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores the UAE's human trafficking market at 8.5 out of 10; the US State Department rates it Tier 2, its grade for governments that do not fully meet its minimum standards and are making efforts to do so.

The scale of abuse behind the UAE's online reports is not known. The UN finding about Al-Bureiqa has not been followed by any prosecution in this record.

BGD.story:
Most of the Bangladesh record concerns girls taken out of the country for sex. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says traffickers exploit Bangladeshi women and girls in the sex trade in India, Pakistan and Gulf countries, and observers estimate that children make up 40 per cent of the Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims exploited abroad. In India, the same report says, traffickers recruit significant numbers of Bangladeshi and Nepali women and girls. In Kolkata's largest red-light area, the young women freed in a 2015 police raid were from Nepal and all held fake adult identity papers, which the charity International Justice Mission said traffickers issue to underage girls.

A second form is inside the country, near Cox's Bazar, where more than one million Rohingya refugees live in 33 camps. The UN fact-finding mission on Myanmar found that Myanmar's army raped hundreds of Rohingya women and girls during its 2017 'clearance operations'. In the camps, the 2025 US report says tourists have increased demand for sexual exploitation, including of Rohingya girls, and the record names traffickers, recruitment agents and armed groups in the camps among those involved. It reports corrupt policing in the camps and calls official complicity a significant concern.

Bangladesh was also a source of children for adoption abroad. A Dutch government committee chaired by Tjibbe Joustra found 'serious violations' in adoptions from Bangladesh and other countries between 1967 and 1997/98, and found that Dutch officials knew of wrongdoing for years and did not act; the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021. A Norwegian committee that reported in 2026 on adoptions from 12 countries, which this map's records link to Bangladesh, found falsified documents and payments to orphanages tied to the number of children adopted.

Prosecution has fallen. Bangladeshi courts convicted 103 traffickers in the 2025 report period, down from 407. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores state-embedded criminal actors at 7 out of 10 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 4.08. Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 697,412 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to Bangladesh in 2024, but there is no representative survey data for South Asia to show how many children are abused online.

Girls are still taken to India and the Gulf, and Rohingya girls in the camps are exploited under corrupt policing. How many children were affected by the adoption abuses has not been counted for Bangladesh.

CAF.story:
In the Central African Republic, most of the record concerns children abused by foreign soldiers sent to protect them and by armed groups and government forces fighting there.

Between December 2013 and June 2014, boys aged about 8 to 13 sheltering in the displaced persons' camp at Bangui's M'Poko airport said soldiers, mostly from France's Operation Sangaris and also from Chad and Equatorial Guinea, abused them, often in exchange for food or money. Under the UN mission MINUSCA, allegations at Dékoa against Gabonese and Burundian troops led to interviews with about 136 alleged victims, 48 per cent of the victims the UN recorded in 2016. Human Rights Watch linked rapes near Bambari airport in 2015 to the period when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded it. UN tables list 15 child victims in allegations against troops from DR Congo. In 2024 the UN recorded 13 child victims in MINUSCA.

Only the country that sent a soldier can prosecute him; the UN can only send troops home. Press accounts say 41 Dékoa troops were sent home uncharged. The DR Congo battalion withdrew in 2016, though it is unclear whether the allegations were the main reason, and the UN sent home all its Gabonese personnel, about 450 in 2021. French judges closed the Sangaris case in 2018 without charging anyone. An independent panel chaired by Marie Deschamps found in 2015 that the report on the M'Poko boys was passed 'from inbox to inbox' and that three senior UN officials abused their authority; staff worried more about whether it had been leaked to France than about acting on it. Anders Kompass, the UN official who passed it to France, was suspended.

Armed groups also abuse and abduct children. The Lord's Resistance Army, an armed group that began in northern Uganda, moved into the country from 2008 and abducted thousands in the region. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 114 girls, 58 of them by the CPC armed-group coalition and 35 by government and pro-government forces, and the abduction of 141 children, most for recruitment or sexual violence. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores state-embedded criminal actors at 9 out of 10 and resilience to organised crime at 2.08.

No foreign soldier in this record has been convicted, and peacekeeper abuse is still reported each year. The UN Secretary-General said in 2025 that violations by government and pro-government forces were rising.

COG.story:
The Republic of Congo appears in this record mainly as the home country of UN peacekeepers accused of abusing children abroad. Human Rights Watch documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by peacekeepers of the UN mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) in the town of Bambari, including a 14-year-old girl who said she was gang-raped near the airport. Survivors believed the soldiers came from the Republic of Congo or DR Congo, and most incidents took place between September and December 2015, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport. Under UN rules, only the country that sent a soldier can prosecute him; the UN can only send troops home. This record holds no Congolese prosecution.

Little is documented about abuse of children inside the country. The US State Department rates it Tier 2 Watch List, one step above its lowest grade. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores state-embedded criminal actors at 8.5 out of 10 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 3.08. Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 6,351 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to the country in 2024, and there is no representative survey data for West and Central Africa.

Whether the Bambari soldiers were investigated at home is not on record, and abuse of children in the country itself has not been documented here.

DOM.story:
Two forms of child sexual abuse run through the Dominican record, and in both, people from abroad play a central part. One is the sale of children, mostly teenage girls, to visitors in tourist towns. The US State Department's 2025 report says girls are frequently exploited on streets, in parks and on beaches, and non-governmental groups link the rising number of child victims to weak regulation of tourism. In the cases on record, local pimping rings supplied them. In 2015 Dominican authorities, working with US Homeland Security Investigations, staged a fake 'sex party' in the tourist town of Sosúa, freed 29 victims, 20 of them aged 14 to 17, and charged seven Dominicans. On the north coast, around Puerto Plata and Sosúa, US men have been prosecuted at home under the PROTECT Act, a US law that lets American courts try citizens for abusing children abroad.

The other form is abuse by foreign Catholic clergy, which the church dealt with by moving the accused out of the country. The Polish archbishop Józef Wesołowski, the Pope's ambassador (nuncio) to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled to the Vatican in August 2013, before Dominican prosecutors opened their investigation that September. The Vatican later told Polish prosecutors he could not be extradited. A church court found him guilty and removed him from the priesthood in 2014; a Vatican prosecutor charged him in 2015 with abusing children in the Dominican Republic, but he died before trial. A Polish priest who had worked there, Wojciech Gil, returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic. Polish police arrested him using Dominican evidence, and in 2015 he was sentenced to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic and two in Poland.

The country is also a route out of Haiti. After the 2010 earthquake, ten members of New Life Children's Refuge, a Baptist group from Idaho, were arrested trying to take 33 Haitian children across the border; its leader was convicted of arranging irregular travel.

Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 181,140 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to the country in 2024, or 1,585.1 per 100,000 people. Walk Free, a research group, estimates 72,000 people in modern slavery of all forms.

Children are still sold to visitors in tourist areas. The clergy cases were tried abroad or not at all, and no Dominican court tried either man.

FJI.story:
The Fiji record is about Catholic clergy accused of abusing children, some of whom were sent to Fiji from Australia and New Zealand after allegations arose there. In July 2020 the news service 1News reported about 1,300 alleged cases of child abuse involving clergy in Fiji, some of them concerning clergy from those two countries, and a survivor advocate said Fiji was a common destination for transferred clergy.

The best documented move is that of Julian Fox, a priest of the Salesians, a Catholic religious order present in more than 130 countries. The order moved him to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating abuse allegations against him. The Catholic Church in Fiji knew of the allegations nine years before he was charged, and he was jailed in Australia in 2015. Until December 2019 the Vatican handled abuse cases under a rule of secrecy known as the pontifical secret, and national inquiries elsewhere found that bishops moved accused clergy and avoided the police.

The US State Department rates Fiji Tier 2 Watch List. Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 2,713 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to Fiji in 2024.

How many of the roughly 1,300 alleged cases involve transferred clergy, and whether any were investigated in Fiji, is not known from this record.

GNB.story:
This map holds no documented case, flow or network for Guinea-Bissau, so what is known comes only from international ratings. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores state-embedded criminal actors at 8.5 out of 10 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 2.67 out of 10. It scores the human trafficking market at 5.5. Walk Free, a research group, estimates 9,000 people in modern slavery of all forms. Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 437 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to the country in 2024, and Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data on online abuse for West and Central Africa.

None of these measures counts child sexual abuse directly, and no inquiry or prosecution is on record here.

HRV.story:
The Croatian record is mainly about Catholic priests who abused children and courts that gave them short sentences. In 2000 a court convicted Fr Ivan Čuček of abusing 37 girls, and the Supreme Court cut his three-year sentence to 18 months. The first Croatian priest to serve prison time was Fr Drago Ljubičić of Rab, jailed in 2007 for three years for molesting five teenage boys.

Time limits on prosecution have kept older cases out of court. Fr Nediljko Ivanov of Bibinje abused children between 1983 and 1991, and the abuse was reported in 2012, too late for a criminal case. He became the first priest convicted by a Croatian church court, which ordered only prayer, fasting and an apology, and he continued to say Mass. Church courts apply the church's own law and cannot jail anyone. Until December 2019 the Vatican handled such cases under a rule of secrecy known as the pontifical secret.

Croatia is also linked in this map's records to international police operations against online abuse, a New Zealand-led operation that by 2022 had opened 836 cases worldwide and safeguarded 146 children, and the 2025 operation against Kidflix, a paid streaming site for abuse videos with 1.8 million users. Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 8,861 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to Croatia in 2024.

This record contains no national inquiry into abuse in Croatian church institutions, so the number of victims has not been measured, and cases as old as Ivanov's can no longer be prosecuted.

ISL.story:
The Icelandic record covers abuse at a Catholic school and abuse material stored on servers in the country.

The school was Landakotsskóli, run by the Catholic Church in Iceland. A commission set up by the church and chaired by Hjördís Hákonardóttir reported in November 2012 that its principal, Rev. Ágúst Georg, and a teacher, Margrét Müller, had abused pupils. Of 30 former pupils and summer-camp children it questioned, 8 said they had been sexually abused and 27 described mental abuse. The commission found that Bishop Joannes Gijsen had destroyed a letter from a man who said the priest abused him. In 2015 the Althing, Iceland's parliament, passed Act No. 117/2015, which extended the state's compensation scheme for abuse in institutions to former Landakotsskóli pupils.

Online, Iceland's part is mainly as a host. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, acted on 7,455 web addresses on servers in Iceland, 2 per cent of all those it acted on worldwide. Iceland is also linked in this map's records to two European-led police operations in 2025, one against Kidflix, a paid streaming site for abuse videos with 1.8 million users, and Operation Cumberland, against a platform selling AI-generated abuse images, for which Europol noted a lack of national laws. Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 1,363 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to Iceland in 2024, or 352.6 per 100,000 people.

International ratings score Iceland low for organised crime. The US State Department rates it Tier 1, and the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores its state-embedded criminal actors at 1 out of 10.

Former Landakotsskóli pupils can now claim state compensation. Abuse material continues to be found on Icelandic servers.

KEN.story:
The largest part of the Kenyan record is the sale of children for sex on the coast, to foreign tourists and to Kenyans. A 2006 study by UNICEF and Kenya's Ministry of Home Affairs of four beach resort areas found that up to 30 per cent of girls aged 12 to 18 there were involved in casual sex work and that two to three thousand children were in full-time commercial sex. Italian, German and Swiss tourists made up 44 per cent of the clients and Kenyans 38 per cent. The US State Department's 2025 report cites a 2023 study by a non-governmental group estimating that more than 2,000 children were exploited in Kilifi and Kwale counties, increasingly in private villas and holiday homes and less in hotels. It names family members, taxi drivers and recruiters among those involved.

Children are also brought to Kenya and moved within it. The same report describes cross-border rings taking women and underage girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi for domestic servitude or sex, and truck drivers, miners and fishermen on Lake Victoria exploiting children. In Nairobi, a 2020 BBC Africa Eye investigation found children taken from homeless mothers and sold for about £350 to £550, street clinics selling newborns, and a social worker at the government-run Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital who sold an abandoned baby to undercover reporters using legitimate transfer papers; the BBC said he appeared to keep his job.

A commission chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga for SOS Children's Villages, an international charity that runs children's homes, confirmed serious allegations of sexual abuse and cover-ups in several of its national associations in 2023, and Kenya is among the countries named in its report.

In 2006 Vice President Moody Awori accepted the coastal study and said police and communities had failed to enforce the law. The 2025 US report notes continuing concerns of official complicity with no reported action against complicit officials. Some foreign offenders are tried at home. A British court jailed Keith Morris for 18.5 years for 10 sexual offences against vulnerable children in Kenya, one of about eight British prosecutions for offences abroad since 1997. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores state-embedded criminal actors at 8 out of 10.

Children are still sold for sex on the coast. Officials linked to trafficking have not faced action on record.

LKA.story:
Most of the Sri Lankan record concerns babies sold for adoption abroad in the 1980s. Brokers, and hospital doctors and nurses acting for Western adoption agencies, bought babies or took them from hospitals and handed them to paid 'acting mothers', who posed as the birth mothers in court. The record counts 11,000 children. About 4,000 went to the Netherlands, and others to Britain, Sweden, Germany and Denmark. A 1987 police raid on one of these 'baby farms' found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions', and Sri Lanka imposed a temporary ban on foreign adoptions. In 2017 a Dutch television documentary led Health Minister Rajitha Senaratne to admit that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announce an inquiry.

The receiving countries have since found that their own officials knew. A Dutch committee found 'serious violations' in adoptions from Sri Lanka and other countries and that officials had known of wrongdoing for years; the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021. Switzerland's government acknowledged irregularities by its authorities in 2020 and 2023, whose decisions had often rested on falsified documents and children wrongly presented as orphans, and recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption at the end of 2024.

Sri Lanka has also protected its own soldiers. Between 2004 and 2007, members of its army contingent with the UN mission in Haiti exploited children; the UN's internal oversight office found the abuse 'frequent' and at 'virtually every location' where they were deployed, and an Associated Press investigation found at least 134 soldiers had exploited at least nine children. Only Sri Lanka could prosecute them. Its authorities judged the acts 'consensual', 114 soldiers were sent home, and none was jailed.

At home, the national child protection agency was slow to act. Complaints about a Buddhist monk running a children's home in Vavuniya for war-affected Tamil children reached the National Child Protection Authority from 2010; he was arrested in 2013 only after protests by local child protection officers, and the authority then told prosecutors not to oppose his bail.

The 2025 US State Department report says boys and girls are reportedly exploited for foreign offenders in coastal areas; the government convicted six traffickers and identified seven child victims that year.

No Sri Lankan inquiry finding on the baby farms is on record, and none of the soldiers sent home from Haiti was jailed.

MHL.story:
The Marshall Islands record is about babies taken to the United States for adoption through a paid scheme run by a US official. Paul Petersen, the elected assessor of Maricopa County in Arizona and an adoption lawyer, paid recruiters to bring pregnant Marshallese women to Arizona, Utah and Arkansas. Forty women were moved in this way between 2015 and 2019. He paid the women about $10,000 each to give up their babies and charged adoptive couples about $35,000. The Compact of Free Association, the treaty that lets Marshallese citizens travel to the United States, bars travel there for adoption. He also obtained about $814,000 in Arizona Medicaid funds, the state's public health insurance, for the women by fraud.

The first complaint on record dates from 2017, and the scheme kept running for two more years. Petersen was charged in Utah, Arizona and Arkansas in October 2019, pleaded guilty in all three in June 2020 to human smuggling and fraud, and was sentenced in December 2020 by a federal court in Arkansas to more than six years in prison.

Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 72 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to the country in 2024.

Petersen has been convicted and sentenced. The record does not say what became of the children or whether their adoptions were reviewed.

MYS.story:
The Malaysian record covers children abused in homes run by a business linked to a banned religious movement, schoolgirls abused by logging workers in Sarawak, babies sold through online brokers, and abuse material stored on Malaysian servers.

The largest case concerns children's homes run by Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB), a company linked to the banned Al-Arqam movement. In September 2024 police raided 20 of its charity homes in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, rescued 402 children aged 1 to 17 and arrested 171 adults; by October the number of children rescued had reached 625. Police said they had received 41 reports about the group since 2011. Three religious school assistants in Kuala Pilah were charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing five children, another with sexually assaulting four boys, and police said the investigation pointed to organised crime and human trafficking.

In Sarawak the abusers on record were workers of logging companies, and the victims were girls of the Penan people. A team from the Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development found in 2008 that timber workers had raped or tried to abuse Penan schoolgirls, some as young as 10, including girls given lifts to school in logging trucks. The report was made public only in 2009, after the Associated Press obtained it, and it named no company. Sarawak police said three complaints had been investigated the year before without enough evidence to prosecute.

Babies are also sold. A 2016 Al Jazeera investigation found babies advertised online with photos and sold for thousands of dollars, with buyers choosing by gender, race and skin colour; some went to couples, and others, it reported, to traffickers. Among those giving up babies were immigrant sex workers, who cannot legally bear children in Malaysia.

Malaysia also hosts abuse material. The Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, acted on 17,046 web addresses on Malaysian servers in 2025, 5 per cent of its total, as in 2024. Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 111,696 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to Malaysia in 2024. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores its human trafficking market at 7.5 out of 10 and state-embedded criminal actors at 7.

The record does not give the outcome of the GISB charges. The Penan cases did not reach court, and no logging company has been named.

OMN.story:
Little is documented about the abuse of children in Oman. The one item this map holds for the country is that Oman has banned the online game platform Roblox since 2020. In 2025 Qatar and Kuwait blocked the same platform after parents and community groups raised concerns about children's safety on it.

Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 37,109 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to Oman in 2024, or 702.6 per 100,000 people. These are reports of suspected material, and Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data for the Middle East and North Africa that would show how many children are abused. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores Oman's human trafficking market at 7 out of 10, and Walk Free, a research group, estimates 33,000 people in modern slavery of all forms; neither figure is specific to children.

No inquiry, prosecution or trafficking flow involving children in Oman is on record here.

PRK.story:
There is almost no documented information on the abuse of children in North Korea. The US CyberTipline, which receives reports of suspected online child abuse from technology companies, recorded 12 reports for the country, the figure this map gives for both 2024 and 2025. That number reflects how few people in North Korea can use American apps and says nothing about how many children are abused.

The broader ratings are at or near the bottom of their scales. The US State Department rates North Korea Tier 3, its lowest grade. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores state-embedded criminal actors at 10 out of 10, the human trafficking market at 9 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 1.63. Walk Free, a research group, estimates 2,696,000 people in modern slavery of all forms, or 104.6 per 1,000 people. None of these figures is specific to children.

No case, inquiry or flow involving children in North Korea is on record here.

SAU.story:
Saudi Arabia appears in this record mainly as a destination for children brought from abroad to beg. The US State Department's 2025 report on Ethiopia says traffickers exploit Ethiopian women and children in forced begging in Saudi Arabia, sometimes through organised begging rings, and that reports of official complicity continued in Ethiopia. The same year, its report on Indonesia described tourists from the Middle East paying for short 'contract marriages' with girls as young as nine in Puncak, West Java; this map's records link that flow to Saudi Arabia, though the report names only the region.

Little is recorded about abuse of children inside the country. Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 385,745 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to Saudi Arabia in 2024, or 1,092.8 per 100,000 people. These are reports of suspected material, and Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data for the Middle East and North Africa that would show how many children are abused. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores the human trafficking market at 8.5 out of 10, state-embedded criminal actors at 9 and resilience to organised crime at 3.79. Walk Free, a research group, estimates 740,000 people in modern slavery of all forms, or 21.3 per 1,000; this figure is not specific to children.

Ethiopian children are still reported in begging rings in Saudi Arabia. No Saudi inquiry or prosecution concerning children is on record here.

STP.story:
This map holds no documented case, flow or network for São Tomé and Príncipe. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores its human trafficking market at 1.5 out of 10, state-embedded criminal actors at 3 and resilience to organised crime at 4.79. Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 695 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to the country in 2024, or 295.1 per 100,000 people, and Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data on online abuse for West and Central Africa.

None of these measures counts child sexual abuse directly, and no inquiry or prosecution is on record here.

TKM.story:
This map holds no documented case, flow or network for Turkmenistan, and very little information from the country reaches international reporting systems. The US CyberTipline, which receives reports of suspected online child abuse from technology companies, recorded 591 reports for Turkmenistan, the figure this map gives for both 2024 and 2025, or 7.9 per 100,000 people.

The broader ratings are poor. The US State Department rates Turkmenistan Tier 2 Watch List, one step above its lowest grade. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores its human trafficking market at 8 out of 10, state-embedded criminal actors at 9 and resilience to organised crime at 2.17. Walk Free, a research group, estimates 72,000 people in modern slavery of all forms. None of these figures is specific to children.

No inquiry or prosecution concerning children in Turkmenistan is on record here.

UKR.story:
In Ukraine, the largest part of the record concerns children in state institutions, who are recruited from them into the sex trade, and children harmed in Russia's war.

In the record, state orphanages, boarding schools and homes for children with disabilities supply traffickers. Disability Rights International, a US advocacy group, visited 33 institutions between 2012 and 2015. La Strada Ukraine, an anti-trafficking charity, told it that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution was 'the most typical scheme' and that sexual exploitation in institutions usually began around age 13, often started by staff. An official of the International Organization for Migration said most documented cases began in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. The US State Department's 2025 report says officials of several state-run residential institutions were allegedly complicit or negligent in the trafficking of children in their care, and that no complicit official had been convicted for the eighth year running.

Ukraine has also been a place where abuse images were made for sale abroad. From 2001 a Kyiv modelling agency with branches in Kharkiv and Simferopol recruited children through adverts and sold sexualised images of them worldwide; police raided it in 2004, and the legal outcome was described as lenient. Producers in Crimea supplied Azov Films, a Toronto company that sold films of children to customers in more than 50 countries until police raided it.

Girls from Ukraine were also taken abroad. Human Rights Watch in 2002 and Amnesty International in 2004 found women and girls from Ukraine, Moldova and Romania trafficked into bars and brothels in post-war Bosnia and Kosovo, where foreign soldiers, UN police and contractors were among the buyers.

A UN commission of inquiry found that Russian forces committed rape and other sexual violence, and documented children raped, tortured and unlawfully confined. Ukraine's official Children of War platform records 23 children sexually abused. In 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova for the unlawful deportation of children; Ukraine counts 20,651 children deported or forcibly displaced and 2,752 returned. The 2025 US report says children evacuated from at least 195 institutions are at high risk and refugee children are vulnerable abroad. Ukrainian courts convicted 24 traffickers in 2024, six of them with prison terms.

Children in institutions remain exposed to traffickers, and most deported children have not returned. The report calls child sex trafficking in Ukraine underreported.

XKX.story:
The Kosovo record concerns women and girls brought into the country for forced prostitution after foreign troops and administrators arrived. Amnesty International reported in May 2004 that Kosovo had become a major destination for this trade since NATO's force (KFOR) and the UN administration came in 1999. Criminal networks brought women and girls mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia through Serbia, and also abducted local girls.

The buyers in Amnesty's account were largely foreign. It said the international presence, including KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff, generated 80 per cent of traffickers' income at the time. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'. Soldiers serving abroad can be tried only by their own countries, and Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel at home.

The record counts women and girls together, so the number of children involved is not known. Technology companies sent the US CyberTipline 3,364 reports of suspected online child abuse linked to Kosovo in 2024. The US State Department rates Kosovo Tier 2, and Walk Free, a research group, estimates 14,000 people in modern slavery of all forms.

No soldier is on record as tried for these offences. The record does not describe the trade after 2004.
